records.name: Liberia
records.summary: Liberia is dangerous for trans visitors. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never colonised); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no LGR.

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Oct 2024): Rep. Johnson N. Williams is seeking lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer; related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex — documents active legislative threat beyond the existing statute.

UNDP/OHCHR 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia Country Report' (April 2020): participatory review and analysis of the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia.

NPR (9 Apr 2012, 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight'): anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The Guardian (19 Mar 2012, Monrovia): Nobel Peace Prize president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview; her remarks drew international comment on Liberia's stance (Blair declined to comment).

records.name: Djibouti
records.summary: Djibouti is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague “good morals” provisions (Arts 353/354) make homosexuality “de facto illegal” in practice; no anti-discrimination law, no LGR, no community infrastructure; authoritarian state with US/French bases but no rights space.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): penal code §§ 353–354 refer vaguely to 'good morals' with no explicit criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, yet their at-a-glance table still marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; current-fact: still no explicit offence, but 'obscene acts'/public morality provisions are used against people.

Wikipedia overview (current): legality of same-sex conduct is ambiguous — no law says either way, but authorities can prosecute public same-sex conduct under 'good morals' provisions, so it is treated as de facto illegal; discrimination protection exists in employment only; no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report, Djibouti SOGIESC section: law does not explicitly criminalise consensual LGBTQI+ conduct, but status and conduct are taboo; a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable — complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH); no legal prohibition of SOGI discrimination; pervasive social and religious intolerance makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) - baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request DJI104070.E (research 2009–Mar 2012, via ecoi.net): documentation on treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti was scarce across all consulted sources, leaning on the US 2010 country report — a dated historical baseline showing how little legal/protection framework and support services existed in that period.
